hook.text: An interval tells you which values are plausible. A test asks about one value in particular... usually, could the effect be zero?

checkout.text: Say a new checkout converts at eleven point four percent, and the old one at ten point one.

free.text: But noise makes gaps for free. So the real question is this. If there were no difference at all, how often would chance alone hand you a gap this big?

null.text: A test starts from the boring answer: nothing is going on. That's the null hypothesis. The alternative says there's a real effect.

surprise.text: Then it asks one thing. If the null were true, would data like mine be surprising?

verdict.text: Very surprising, and you reject the null. Ordinary, and you fail to reject it.

court-in.text: If that sounds like a trial, it is one.

court.text: The null is the defendant, presumed innocent until the evidence says otherwise.

bar.text: Beyond reasonable doubt becomes alpha, the bar the evidence has to clear. Usually five percent, and set before the trial begins.

guilty.text: Clear the bar, and the verdict is guilty: reject the null. Fall short, and it's not guilty.

innocent.text: And not guilty never means innocent. Failing to reject the null doesn't prove it. The evidence just wasn't strong enough.

steps.text: An app claims its users walk eight thousand steps a day. Forty of them average seven thousand, four hundred and fifty-three.

set.text: The null says the true mean is eight thousand. Alpha is five percent, fixed now, before anything is computed.

tstat.text: The test statistic measures the gap in units of noise. Here, t is minus two point two four.

pval.text: If the claim were true, a gap at least this big would turn up three percent of the time. That's the p-value.

reject.text: Three is under five, so we reject the claim. Not because we know the true mean, but because eight thousand is hard to believe.

sides-in.text: And notice: at least this big, in either direction.

sides.text: Higher or lower would both count, so surprise lives in both tails. A five percent test puts two and a half percent in each, beyond one point nine six.

onesided.text: A one-sided test spends all five percent in one tail, so its cutoff is nearer, at one point six four five.

early.text: That's an easier bar to clear... which is exactly why the side has to be chosen before you see the data.

coin-in.text: So what is that three percent, exactly?

coin.text: Take a simpler case. A friend's coin lands heads sixty-two times in a hundred flips.

fair.text: Assume it's fair, and simulate a hundred flips, a hundred thousand times over. That pile is the null distribution.

far.text: Sixty-two sits twelve from the middle. So does thirty-eight. Now count every run at least that far out.

area.text: Two point one percent of them. That's all a p-value is: the share of the null world at least as extreme as what you saw.

isnt-in.text: And that tells you what it can't be.

isnt.text: A p-value is NOT the chance the null is true. It was computed by assuming the null.

swap.text: The chance of the data, given the null, isn't the chance of the null, given the data. Swap them, and you've made the prosecutor's fallacy.

size.text: Nor is it the size of an effect. Hold a tiny effect fixed, and only grow the sample.

collapse.text: Twenty per group, p is point eight three. A thousand, point zero zero zero four. A hundred thousand, and it prints as zero.

same.text: The effect never changed. Only how much data could see it.

hack-in.text: Which leads to the easiest way to fool yourself.

uniform.text: When the null is true, a p-value is just a random number. Every value from zero to one is equally likely.

twenty.text: So run twenty tests where nothing is real, and you should expect one under point zero five.

fourteen.text: Here, it's test fourteen, at point zero three three.

hacked.text: Report only that one, and you've turned luck into a discovery. That's p-hacking.

odds.text: Across twenty tests, the chance that at least one fires is sixty-four percent.

peek.text: Peeking at a running experiment, and stopping when p dips under point zero five, does the same thing, one look at a time.

cure.text: The cure is deciding before you look: the question, the sample and the analysis, all fixed in advance.

bonferroni.text: Or raise the bar for every test. Twenty tests sharing five percent means each one needs point zero zero two five.

errors-in.text: But even a test played fairly can be wrong, in two ways.

grid.text: Cross what's true with what you decide, and you get four outcomes.

typeone.text: Reject a null that's true, and that's a false alarm, a Type One error. Its rate is alpha.

typetwo.text: Miss an effect that's real, and that's a Type Two error, with rate beta.

power.text: The cell beside it is power: the chance of catching an effect that's really there.

sim.text: Power is easiest to see by counting. Plant a real effect of half a standard deviation, test thirty per group, and repeat two thousand times.

coinflip.text: Forty-seven and a half percent of the runs reject. Finding an effect that's really there is a coin flip.

trade.text: Lower alpha to cut false alarms, and you miss even more. With the sample fixed, pushing one error down pushes the other up.

more.text: Only more data shrinks both. Forty per group catches this effect sixty-one percent of the time. Eighty catches ninety.

target.text: Studies are usually designed for at least eighty percent.

ab.text: That's why an A-B test is sized before it starts. To catch a lift from ten percent to twelve, with eighty percent power, takes three thousand, eight hundred and forty-one users in each arm.

halve.text: Halve the lift, to eleven, and it takes fourteen thousand, seven hundred and fifty-one. Nearly four times as many.

curse.text: And low power does worse than miss. Test a real effect of point three with fifteen per group, and only twelve percent of runs reach significance.

inflate.text: Those winners average point eight five, nearly three times the truth. Only the runs that noise exaggerated made it through.

t-in.text: Every test in those simulations was a t-test.

ratio.text: Its statistic is a ratio: the gap you observed, over the noise in that gap, its standard error.

big.text: A big t means the gap dwarfs the noise. A small one means it's the size of an ordinary wobble.

designs.text: It comes in three designs: one group against a target, two separate groups, or the same units measured twice.

pairs.text: That last one matters more than it looks. Twenty-five patients' blood pressure, before and after a program.

unpaired.text: Compare the two columns as separate groups, and the differences between people drown the change. p is point one one five.

paired.text: Test each patient's own change instead, and the noise collapses. t is ten, and p is under one in a billion.

own.text: Same data. Each patient just became their own control.

groups-in.text: With more than two groups, the tempting move is a t-test for every pair.

groups.text: Five groups make ten pairs. Draw all five from the same process, and some pair comes up significant in thirty-two percent of trials.

once.text: That's the many-looks problem again. ANOVA asks once: do any of the means differ?

ftest.text: Its F statistic is the spread between the group means, over the spread within the groups.

warehouses.text: Three warehouses' delivery times give an F of twelve. At least one of them differs... but ANOVA won't say which.

chi.text: When the data are categories, not numbers, a test compares counts instead. Here's device against churn, for six hundred users.

expected.text: If device made no difference, about eighty-seven mobile users would have churned.

observed.text: A hundred and three did. Desktop came in well under its share.

related.text: Chi-square adds up how far every cell strays from what was expected. Here it's about twelve, with a p of point zero zero three.

corr-in.text: And when both columns are numbers, you ask whether they move together.

corr.text: A correlation runs from minus one to one. Pearson's r measures how close the points sit to a straight line.

curve.text: On a curve that always rises, it says point eight seven. Spearman's rho works on ranks, so it only asks whether y keeps rising. Point nine nine.

ushape.text: And an r near zero isn't the same as no relationship. On this U-shape, r is minus point zero three, though y depends entirely on x.

ranks.text: Ranks rescue tests, too. Two support queues, each with three monster tickets that dragged on for hours.

welch.text: Those outliers swell the noise, and Welch's t-test sees nothing. p is point seven two.

mwu.text: Mann-Whitney ranks the values instead, and finds the shift. p is point zero three three.

line.text: A rank doesn't care how far out an outlier is, only where it stands in line.

next.text: Every test here answers one narrow question: could the effect be zero? Not how big it is... or whether it means what it seems to.
